match.reason: No bank point plans a data collection by deciding what to collect, from whom, how and why; the closest, market research, only covers choosing between primary and secondary data within a business context, which is related but narrower.

draft.title: Planning data collection
card: Start with the purpose: the question you want to answer. The purpose decides what data to collect, from whom and how.
Choose the group to collect from. It must be the people or things the question is about. Asking the wrong group gives data that cannot answer the question.
Choose the method, such as a survey, an interview or counting records. The method must suit the data. Numbers like age or cost suit a survey or records.

Think about the audience, the people who will read the results. They decide how simple the data and its display should be. Example: a council asks how people travel to the pool. It should ask pool visitors, not only people at a bus stop.
draft.remember: Plan from the purpose: what to collect, from whom, how, and for which audience.

a.q: A gym wants to know why members cancel. What is the best group to collect data from?
opts: Members who have recently cancelled
Members who visit the gym every day
People walking past the gym
The gym's newest staff members
a.why: The question is about members who cancel, so the data must come from people who cancelled. Daily visitors are members, but they are unlikely to be the ones leaving, so they cannot explain cancelling.
a.clue: Who has actually done the thing you are asking about?

b.q: Priya runs a café in Geelong. She wants to know which new menu items her customers would buy. What is the best plan?
opts: Ask café customers to rate the new items after tasting
Ask her friends to guess which items would sell
Count the total daily sales of the existing menu
Ask people in a shopping centre about their favourite foods
b.why: The purpose is customers' views on the new items, so she must ask her own customers, and tasting gives them a real basis to rate. Existing sales say nothing about items not yet on the menu, so that option does not match the purpose.
b.clue: Match the group and the data to the question being asked.

b.best: Ask café customers to rate the new items after tasting

problems.detail: The pool example sits under the audience bullet but shows choosing the right group to collect from, not thinking about the audience. This could confuse students about what 'audience' means. Move it to the group bullet or give an audience example.
'They decide how simple the data and its display should be' suggests the audience makes the decision. It is the planner who decides, with the audience in mind.

proposal.title: Planning data collection
card: Start with the purpose: the question you want to answer. The purpose decides what data to collect, from whom and how.
Collect from the people or things the question is about. Example: to learn how people travel to the pool, ask pool visitors, not only people at a bus stop.
Choose a method that suits the data, such as a survey, an interview or counting records. Numbers like age or cost suit a survey or records.
Think about the audience, the people who will read the results. The planner chooses how simple the data and its display should be with them in mind, such as plain graphs for the public.
